summary: Examines whether existing GMPLS routing and signaling mechanisms can be used to set up ODUk label switched paths over ODUCn links in optical transport networks beyond 100 Gbit/s, as defined by ITU-T G.709. It is an applicability study.

plainLanguage.summary: It checks whether the old traffic rules for optical highways still work when the highways get much faster.

questions: how to signal oduk lsps over oducn
subtitle: Adapting existing optical network control protocols for speeds beyond 100 gigabits per second.

tldr.problem: ITU-T updated its Optical Transport Network (OTN) standard in 2016 and 2020 to define new high-speed signals (OTUCn and ODUCn) operating at multiples of 100 Gbit/s. The existing GMPLS routing and signaling protocols for setting up label switched paths (LSPs) were designed for older OTN signals up to 100 Gbit/s, and network operators needed to understand whether these protocols would work with the new, faster signals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes how existing GMPLS mechanisms from RFC 7138 (routing) and RFC 7139 (signaling) map to the new ODUCn/OTUCn signals defined in ITU-T G.709:2020. It concludes that no new extensions are required for routing, and signaling can use existing label formats with only potential future optimizations for very large networks.
tldr.outcome: The analysis shows existing GMPLS protocols are sufficient to control high-speed OTN networks, enabling operators to deploy 100+ Gbit/s optical paths using current tools.

facts.label: New TPN field size in G.709:2020

today: RFC 9376 is an Informational RFC published in March 2023. It remains current as an analysis document: existing GMPLS protocols continue to be sufficient for modern high-speed OTN deployments. The document notes that optimizations to label encoding may become relevant in the future as networks scale to even higher capacities, but this is not yet necessary. No updates to the RFC are known.

sections.title: Scaling OTN to Higher Speeds
sections.content:
The Optical Transport Network (OTN) is a layer of the telecommunications infrastructure that carries digital signals at high speeds. For decades, OTN signals were capped at 100 Gbit/s, defined by standards like ODU4. In 2016, ITU-T updated the G.709 standard to introduce OTUCn and ODUCn signals, where n is a multiplier indicating 100 Gbit/s per unit (so ODUCn can represent 200 Gbit/s, 300 Gbit/s, etc.).

GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a control plane protocol that automatically sets up label switched paths (LSPs), the equivalent of virtual circuits in optical networks. Existing GMPLS specifications (RFC 7138 for routing, RFC 7139 for signaling) were written for OTN signals up to ODU4 (100 Gbit/s). This RFC determines whether these existing protocols can control the new faster signals without modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS controls how data flows through fiber-optic networks. When networks got faster, engineers needed to check if the old control system still worked for the super-fast networks.

sections.title: ODUCn Structure and Multiplexing
sections.content:
An ODUCn signal is constructed from n interleaved ODUC instances, each approximately 100 Gbit/s. ODUCn supports only lower-rate ODUk clients (such as ODU1, ODU2, ODU3, ODU4, or flexible-rate ODUflex). Unlike older OTU signals that could provide path-layer switching, ODUCn and OTUCn perform only section-layer (regeneration) functions.

Each ODUCn has 20*n tributary slots, each offering 5 Gbit/s of capacity. The Multiplex Structure Indicator (MSI) field (40*n bytes) describes which slots are allocated and assigns each to a client signal via a Tributary Port Number (TPN). The RFC notes the TPN field in ITU-T G.709:2020 has 14 bits, while existing GMPLS only supports 12 bits—sufficient for networks up to 40 Tbit/s (n=400), so not immediately urgent.
sections.plainLanguage: The ODUCn is a big pipe divided into smaller slots, each carrying a client signal. GMPLS labels describe which slots belong to which client.

sections.title: GMPLS Signaling and Label Encoding
sections.content:
When GMPLS sets up an ODUk or ODUflex LSP over an ODUCn link, it uses signaling messages to reserve resources. The label (which identifies which slots the LSP uses) is encoded in a Generalized Label object defined in RFC 7139.

The existing label format specifies: a Tributary Port Number (TPN), a length field indicating how many slots are allocated, and a bitmask showing which slots within the OPUCn are assigned. For example, multiplexing an ODU4 (which needs 20 slots) onto an ODUC10 (which has 200 slots total) results in a label with only 20 out of 200 bits set to 1—inefficient for large-n networks. The RFC identifies this as a possible future optimization but notes that existing labels technically work.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS signaling uses a label (like a ticket) to tell each network element which slots of the big pipe belong to a particular connection. The old label format wastes space for very large pipes but still works.

sections.title: TE Links, Routing, and Configuration
sections.content:
GMPLS represents an OTUCn physical link as a Traffic Engineering (TE) link. A TE link can span a single hop (directly between two switches) or multiple hops through regeneration nodes (which terminate OTUCn but pass ODUCn unchanged). The two endpoints of a TE link are configured with the ODUCn link attributes: slot granularity (5 Gbit/s) and the list of available tributary slots.

For routing, the RFC concludes no extensions are needed beyond RFC 7138. The ODUCn link attributes are configured locally at each endpoint; the existing OSPF-TE routing protocol advertises which client ODUs can be multiplexed over it. Only client slot types (1.25 Gbit/s and 2.5 Gbit/s ODUk slots) need to be advertised, not the larger 5 Gbit/s ODUCn slots.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS routes traffic by creating virtual pipes (TE links) between network elements. For ultra-fast networks, the old routing rules still apply; each switch just needs to know what slots are available.

sections.title: Conclusion and Future Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC concludes that GMPLS protocols defined in RFC 7138 and RFC 7139 are sufficient to control ODUCn networks without new extensions. This is significant because it means network operators can deploy 100+ Gbit/s optical paths using protocols and equipment designed a decade earlier.

However, the RFC identifies one area for potential future enhancement: the label encoding becomes inefficient for very large n values (high Tbit/s links), where most bits in the mask are zeros. As n grows beyond 400, a more compact label format may become desirable. The RFC also notes that ODU Virtual Concatenation (VCAT), a legacy approach for transporting sub-100 Gbit/s clients, has been deprecated in the new standard, simplifying network designs.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules still work for the new fast networks. But if networks get even faster in the future, a smarter label format might help.
